newsitem.title: USA: Analysts like emerging markets, LatAm a favorite.
newsitem.headline: Analysts like emerging markets, LatAm a favorite.

text.p: Stocks in most emerging markets have surged so far this year and Latin America should be a favourite target for investors, analysts say.
They said that while rising U.S. interest rates in the second quarter could limit growth in developing markets, the rise would not be enough to cool off strong stock market increases.
"After three years of underperformance, the emerging markets (will) do better in 1997. Indeed, that has already happened," said Geoffrey Dennis, global emerging market strategist at HSBC James Capel.
Emerging markets comprise developing parts of Asia, Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and Eastern Europe.
As of May 2, stock markets in developing countries had risen 8.1 percent so far this year, according to the Morgan Stanley Capital International index.

Latin American markets were up almost 21 percent and Europe, Middle East and African exchanges had risen 16.1 percent. Emerging Asian markets have fallen 0.5 percent, dragging down the emerging market index.
By comparison, the overall world stock market index was up 4.8 percent. The MSCI U.S. index, which shadows the Standard & Poors 500, is up 10.4 percent.
At the company level, emerging markets offer attractive earnings growth with low price/earnings ratios, a measure of a company's earnings power.

"What you are doing is buying cheap stocks at a high growth rate," said Scott Opsal, head of international equities at Invista Capital Management, a unit of Principal Financial Group in Des Moines, Iowa.
"That is a significant advantage over (investing in) the United States."
Although analysts disagree on specifics of how a stock portfolio should be divided among emerging markets, they agree Latin American stocks would be among the strongest performers this year.
"There is lots of growth in (Latin America) ... that is going to spill over into earnings growth," said Douglas Johnson, senior international investment strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"We've sort of moved out of the problems that we've seen in the region" historically, such as high inflation, bloated government payrolls and closed markets, he said.
Favourite picks for investment in the region include Brazil, Mexico and Argentina.
Matthew Merritt, senior global investment strategist at ING Barings, forecast a 34.9 percent return from the Brazilian stock market for the 12 months following 1997's first quarter.

Asian markets outside Japan are expected to continue to lag other developing markets through the second quarter. Their economies have been hit by slowing demand for their exports in part because the Japanese yen has weakened against the dollar, making Japanese goods relatively more attractive.
"Asia has had two years of very disappointing performance," said ING Barings' Merritt.
Analysts were most cautious about Thailand and South Korea, especially in the face of likely increases in interest rates in the second quarter.
The reason for the caution is the two economies' steeply slower growth and stress in their banking systems.
Analysts differed on investment picks in Eastern Europe, Middle East and Africa. Favoured markets include Hungary, Egypt, Russia, South Africa and Israel.

"While a further period of consolidation is likely in the near term, we expect renewed momentum later in the year to drive Eastern European markets considerably higher," Merritt and other analysts wrote in a report.
